newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appoints new spokesman for legal issues.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appoints new spokesman for legal issues.

text.p: The White House Thursday appointed a new spokesman to deal with the media on legal issues, including those related to Whitewater and Travel Office investigations as well as campaign financing.
Lanny Davis, a partner in the Washington law firm of Patton Boggs since 1978, would join the staff as special counsel effective Dec. 9, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said in a written statement.
He replaces Mark Fabiani, who recently left the counsel's office after serving as spokesman on legal issues for the past 18 months. Fabiani will head an urban renewal project in San Diego.

Davis would "serve as press spokesman on certain legal issues, including those relating to Whitewater and Travel Office investigations, and to recent questions regarding campaign contributions," McCurry said.

Active in the Democratic Party and in national, state and local politics, Davis also has appeared as a private citizen on a number of television and radio programmes to discuss the legal controversies surrounding the White House.

Aside from the independent prosecutor's investigation of Whitewater, the failed Arkansas land deal in which President and Mrs. Clinton were partners and the inquiry into events surrounding the firing of the travel office staff, the White House has found itself on the defensive over Democratic fundraising activities.

The activities of John Huang, who raised $2.5 million in contributions for the party, $600,000 of which has been returned because of questions as to whether it came from foreign sources, have prompted a barrage of inquiries from the media.
The New York Times, in an editorial on Wednesday, urged Attorney General Janet Reno to name a special counsel to investigate the affair. She has already said she would not.
In the process the Times unleashed a blistering attack on a top Clinton confidant, Bruce Lindsey, as well as McCurry.

The newspaper reported that Lindsey had successfully fended off two White House lawyers who wanted Clinton to admit that two Oval Office meetings with Indonesian billionaire James Riady, who once employed Huang, were not simply social visits but also included discussion of trade policy toward Indonesia and China.

In its editorial, the newspaper said if Lindsey did lead the White House to misrepresent the facts, he should resign as deputy White House counsel. It said McCurry "was left with his reliability in tatters" for describing the meetings as purely social.

McCurry, asked to comment, said some elements of the Times' account of the Lindsey story were exaggerated and some were untrue. He described Lindsey as particularly helpful in getting answers to press questions.
